scenes.heading: API Design: REST, OpenAPI & GraphQL
scenes.narration: Let's look at API design in Go, and the three ways to turn a domain into a stable contract clients can build against.

scenes.heading: A good API is a contract
items: REST models the domain as resources, verbs, and status codes
OpenAPI captures that contract as a machine-readable spec
GraphQL exposes one typed graph clients query field by field
scenes.narration: The core idea is that an API is a contract, not just a pile of endpoints. REST models your domain as nouns addressed by URIs, with HTTP verbs and status codes carrying the intent. OpenAPI turns that contract into a spec you can generate docs and typed code from. GraphQL replaces many fixed endpoints with one typed schema the client queries for exactly the fields it wants.

scenes.heading: How each style handles a request
steps: REST: router dispatches to a handler per resource
Handler reads params, does work, writes status + JSON
GraphQL: one endpoint, resolver runs per field
Per-field resolution can explode into N+1 queries
A dataloader batches keys into one bulk query
scenes.narration: At runtime a REST request dispatches through a router to a handler that reads path and query parameters, does its work, and writes a status code plus a JSON body. A GraphQL request instead hits a single endpoint, and the runtime walks the query tree calling one resolver per field. That per-field model is where the classic N-plus-one problem appears, and a dataloader is what collapses those repeated child fetches into a single batched query.

scenes.heading: REST verbs and status codes in Go
scenes.narration: Here the nouns live in the path and the HTTP verb expresses the action, so you never write get-user or create-order in the URL. On a successful create, the handler returns 201 Created with a Location header pointing at the new resource, rather than a bare 200. Setting the status before writing the body, and honoring idempotency for PUT and DELETE, is what lets clients and proxies retry safely and reason about failures.

scenes.text: Never return 200 on failure — clients, proxies, and monitoring key retries and alerts off the status code.
scenes.narration: The one rule to never break: don't return 200 on a failure with an error body. Clients, proxies, and monitoring all key their retry and alerting logic off the status code, so a 200 tells them everything succeeded even as the request failed. Set the correct 4xx or 5xx status before writing the body, and pair it with a consistent error envelope.

scenes.text: Design the contract deliberately, then let tooling enforce it — OpenAPI codegen for REST, dataloaders for GraphQL.
scenes.narration: The through-line across all three: design the contract deliberately, then let tooling enforce it. Spec-first OpenAPI generates typed server interfaces the compiler checks, and dataloaders keep GraphQL from quietly multiplying your database load. Pick cursor pagination for large collections, and the API can evolve for years without breaking the clients built against it.
